clue.text: Apollo's black-out

parts.note: Apollo is the Greek sun god, so his 'black-out' is the moment his light is cut off by the moon passing in front

explanation.surface: A power cut or memory lapse suffered by the god Apollo, or perhaps by a space mission.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apollo' suggests the NASA moon missions, but here he is the sun god; his light going out is the sun being covered.
explanation.definitionFit: When the moon passes in front of the solar disc, the daylight associated with Apollo is blacked out.

clue.text: Furnished with necessary material, 'e made jokes

parts.note: 'e is a dropped-aitch Cockney spelling of 'he', giving just the letter E
to quip is to make a witty remark, so 'made jokes' is the past tense quipped

explanation.surface: Someone who was given the right supplies turned it all into a laughing matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe marks a dropped H: 'e is how 'he' is written for a Cockney speaker, so only the E is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Being fitted out with the gear a task needs is the meaning of being kitted or supplied.

clue.text: Become rapt---& a cure for the egotist?

explanation.surface: Getting absorbed in something might be just what a self-obsessed person needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To be totally absorbed is to forget yourself; and someone obsessed with self would be cured by mislaying that self.

clue.text: Victoria thumbed by Jack — for a lift ?

definitions.text: thumbed by Jack — for a lift

explanation.surface: Someone called Victoria is being offered a ride by a hitch-hiking Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Little Jack Horner 'put in his thumb and pulled out' this fruit from his pie, so Jack thumbs one to lift it out; 'thumbed for a lift' pretends to be hitch-hiking.
explanation.definitionFit: A Victoria is a popular British variety of the fruit; and the nursery-rhyme boy Jack Horner thumbed one out of his Christmas pie.

clue.text: Mixture I smoke is one from Greenland

indicators.note: a mixture is a blend, here of the letters of the words that follow, which are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A pipe smoker's tobacco blend is said to come from the Arctic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixture' reads as pipe tobacco, which is apt beside 'smoke', but it signals rearranging I SMOKE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Inuit people who live in Greenland were long called by this name in English, now often considered offensive.

clue.text: Squanders food

explanation.surface: Someone wastes their meal.
explanation.definitionFit: To waste money or time bit by bit is to fritter it away; battered fried pieces of fruit or vegetable are a dish of the same name.

clue.text: Like Sonny-boy, that bolt from the blue

explanation.surface: A sentimental song's beloved son arrives like a sudden surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sonny Boy' is the Al Jolson song whose child is a gift from above; 'bolt from the blue' is a sudden surprise, here taken as dropping literally from the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Jolson's song presents the little boy as a gift from on high, and an unexpected blessing is likewise described as dropped from the skies.

clue.text: Ayesha sounds such a sport

indicators.note: the word is said in its Norwegian manner, so the sport's name is heard in place of the written one

parts.note: Ayesha is the immortal queen in H. Rider Haggard's novel She, so her name stands for that title

explanation.surface: A woman named Ayesha makes it sound as though she is a great sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Ayesha is Haggard's 'She-who-must-be-obeyed'; the winter sport's name was traditionally pronounced 'shee', its Norwegian way.
explanation.definitionFit: Gliding downhill on long runners is a winter sport named after the runners themselves.

clue.text: Nag one silly for not being grown up

indicators.note: silly means foolish or mixed up, telling us the letters of the two words beside it are to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone is told off for childish nagging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' pretends to describe the nagging; it rearranges NAG ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal term for minority, the period before adulthood, describes a person who is still under age.

clue.text: Comes to this — let down by gum !

definitions.text: Comes to this — let down by gum

parts.words: Comes to this — let down by gum
parts.note: an idiom for failure, preceded by 'comes', is pictured literally as a stamp or label whose glue has failed

explanation.surface: An exasperated speaker says 'by gum!' at being let down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum' looks like a mild Northern English oath, but it is the actual adhesive that has let go; 'come unglued' is an idiom for things going wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: When a plan fails people say it has come apart, as a label does when its adhesive no longer holds.

clue.text: Scot embraces Hindu Queen of Persia

indicators.note: embraces means holds in its arms, so the name wraps around the other piece

parts.note: Ian is a typically Scottish first name, so a Scot is IAN
a rani is a Hindu queen or a raja's wife

explanation.surface: A Scotsman hugs an Indian queen who happens to rule Persia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen of Persia' reads as one title, but the split falls after 'Queen'; 'of Persia' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Persia is the old name for the country now called Iran, so anything from Persia is of that nation.

clue.text: Either way it's opposite the sea front

indicators.note: the word is the same whichever way it is read, forwards or backwards, which these words say

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A seaside town's promenade is described as facing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sea front' suggests a promenade, but it is a ship's bow; the raised deck at the stern is at the opposite end.
explanation.definitionFit: On a sailing ship the raised deck at the stern, the back end, is the farthest point from the bow.

clue.text: Point of some importance for the dabbler's know how

parts.note: S, for south, is one of the compass points
something mattering is significant, of some importance

explanation.surface: A hobbyist is told which issue matters for gaining expertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Point' is a compass point, giving S for south.
explanation.definitionFit: A dabbler has only a slight, superficial knowledge of a subject, a little here and there.

clue.text: Fanciful aim maybe to drink tea, possibly about four

indicators.note: maybe says the word aim could be some other arrangement of its letters

parts.note: gin is an alcoholic drink

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the shuffled tea goes round the number
possibly says tea is to be taken in another letter order

parts.note: IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone's whimsical plan is to have a cup of tea at around four o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' turns AIM into IMA; 'possibly' turns TEA into ATE, which goes 'about' IV. 'four' looks like teatime but is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanciful mind is full of invention and creative ideas, the quality of a strong mental picture-maker.

clue.text: Missile wide of the mark?

parts.note: broad means wide
an arrow is a missile shot from a bow

explanation.surface: An archer's shot misses its target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wide of the mark' reads as a miss; the arrow-shaped mark was stamped on British government property and convicts' clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A government stamp in the shape of an arrowhead was used in Britain to label official stores and prison uniforms.

clue.text: Annexed rabble-rouser's lecture-place, it appears

indicators.note: it appears says the answer shows itself within the run of letters in the words before

explanation.surface: A demagogue has taken over a hall where lectures are given.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'annEXED RAbble'.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greece and Rome a hall or recess with seats was used for discussion and lectures.

clue.text: Palace fortune-telling set

explanation.surface: A royal residence holds a kit for telling the future.
explanation.walkthrough: Each word goes with the answer: Crystal Palace (a London glass exhibition hall, now a district and football club), crystal-ball fortune-telling, and a crystal set (an early radio).
explanation.definitionFit: The word precedes the London glasshouse, the gazer's glass ball, and the simple wireless built around a mineral detector.

clue.text: In open (or might one say sugared ?) fashion

definitions.text: In open (or might one say sugared ?) fashion

parts.words: In open (or might one say sugared ?) fashion
parts.note: the adverb for frankly also sounds like an adverb formed from fruit preserved in sugar

explanation.surface: Something is done openly, or perhaps sweetly.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank speech is given in an open manner; said aloud the word also suggests 'candied-ly', coated in sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking frankly and without concealment is speaking openly.

clue.text: In which a workman need not fear being fired ?

definitions.text: In which a workman need not fear being fired ?

parts.words: In which a workman need not fear being fired ?
parts.note: 'fired' means dismissed in the surface, but literally set alight, which a fireproof suit prevents

explanation.surface: A worker in a secure job does not fear the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fired' looks like losing a job; here it is catching fire, which the fire-resistant mineral fibre once used for protective suits prevents.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous mineral was woven into fireproof protective clothing, now banned for health reasons.

clue.text: Escape of a criminal? Come off it!

explanation.surface: Someone scoffs at news of a criminal's escape.
explanation.definitionFit: A robber's flight from the scene is the classic term; and an exclamation of disbelief means 'you're joking'.

clue.text: "Her pretty feet Like did creep ' (Herrick)

parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing word in Herrick's poem 'Upon her Feet' names the slow creatures her feet are compared to

explanation.surface: A line of Robert Herrick's verse with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem reads 'Her pretty feet / Like snails did creep / A little out'; the answer is the word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet compares her feet peeping from her skirt to slow, shelled molluscs that creep along.

clue.text: Sums up return on a typewriter

indicators.note: return means go back, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: recaps is short for recapitulates, meaning sums up

explanation.surface: A typist totals figures and hits the carriage return key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' looks like the typewriter's carriage return, but it reverses RECAPS. The definition is a key found on a typewriter.
explanation.definitionFit: The long bar that puts a gap between words is one of the keys a typist presses.

clue.text: Drive forward to support the Spanish

parts.note: a prop is a support
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Someone pushes ahead in order to back the Spanish side.
explanation.definitionFit: To push or thrust something onward is to drive it forward.

clue.text: Blow computers---they're naturally dangerous

parts.note: a puff is a blow of breath
adders are machines or people that compute sums

explanation.surface: Someone curses machines that are a hazard by their nature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'computers' are things that add up; the definition is African vipers, dangerous by nature.
explanation.definitionFit: These venomous African vipers, which inflate themselves when threatened, are a natural hazard.

clue.text: A sorry horse-woman?

explanation.surface: A rider is apologising, or a centaur-like figure is sad.
explanation.definitionFit: An old term for a worn-out nag, and also for a disreputable or bad-tempered female.

clue.text: Parting gesture at sea

explanation.surface: Someone says goodbye on a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand raised in farewell when leaving; and a ridge of moving water is what one meets on the ocean.

clue.text: Declare conversion, being acquitted

indicators.note: a conversion is a change of form, so the letters of the clue's first word are made into a new word

explanation.surface: A defendant announces a change of faith on being found not guilty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conversion' suggests religion, but it rearranges DECLARE.
explanation.definitionFit: An accused found not guilty is freed of the charge, as in 'his name was ...'.

clue.text: Lamb loses tail in Bible

indicators.note: loses tail means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Elia was the pen name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A sacrificial lamb in scripture is missing its tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' is Charles Lamb, who wrote as Elia; drop the last letter. The definition is the priest who raised Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: The priest at Shiloh who brought up the young Samuel is a figure in the Old Testament.

clue.text: A grand player-from his score ?

parts.note: a grand is a type of keyboard instrument, and its player reads music from a score, which could also suggest someone who won a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone earning a thousand pounds from their tally in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grand' looks like a thousand pounds and 'score' a game's total, but it is the large piano and the sheet music.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer at the keyboard of a grand reads the notes from printed music.

clue.text: Do they dream of being run over by a train ?

definitions.text: Do they dream of being run over by a train ?

parts.words: Do they dream of being run over by a train ?
parts.note: the beams under the tracks are named like people asleep, and trains do run over them

explanation.surface: Someone wonders about the nightmares of people asleep on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: The timber or concrete beams holding the rails share their name with people asleep, so the clue asks if they dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The cross-beams beneath the rails are literally run over by every passing train.
